summary.text: Splitting by parity, the proof identifies the linear errors \(B_n-eA_n\) with signed factorial-scaled integrals \(\int_0^1 e^x x^a(1-x)^b\,dx\); integration by parts yields the same coupled recurrences as the sequences, and endpoint evaluations establish the initial cases. These integrals are uniformly bounded, so the factorial-scaled errors tend to zero, and positivity of the integer denominators (hence \(A_n\ge1\)) then forces \(B_n/A_n-e\to0\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A_n=A340738(n),\qquad B_n=A340737(n),
\]
where the two sequences have initial values
\[
A_1=1,\quad A_2=2,\qquad B_1=3,\quad B_2=5,
\]
and obey the same parity-dependent recurrence. Thus, for odd indices,
\[
A_n=2A_{n-1}+nA_{n-2},\qquad
B_n=2B_{n-1}+nB_{n-2},
\]
and for even indices,
\[
A_n=\frac{n+2}{2}A_{n-1}-A_{n-2}-\frac{n-2}{2}A_{n-3},
\]
with the identical formula for \(B_n\). The sequences are integer-valued; in the even recurrence, subtraction is initially understood as natural-number subtraction. We prove
\[
\frac{B_n}{A_n}\longrightarrow e,
\]
where \(e=\exp(1)\).

It is convenient to rewrite the recurrences in terms of pairs of consecutive odd and even indices. For every \(m\ge 0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
A_{2m+3}&=2A_{2m+2}+(2m+3)A_{2m+1},\\
B_{2m+3}&=2B_{2m+2}+(2m+3)B_{2m+1},
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{1}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
A_{2m+4}&=(m+3)A_{2m+3}-A_{2m+2}-(m+1)A_{2m+1},\\
B_{2m+4}&=(m+3)B_{2m+3}-B_{2m+2}-(m+1)B_{2m+1}.
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{2}
\]
The expressions in (2) are still, at this point, natural-number subtractions.

We first record that these subtractions do not cause a problem when the recurrences are regarded over the reals. The elementary observation needed is this: if \(a\le c\) and \(b\le c\), then
\[
c\le (m+3)c-b-(m+1)a.                                      \tag{3}
\]
Indeed,
\[
b+(m+1)a+c\le c+(m+1)c+c=(m+3)c,
\]
which implies (3) and also shows that both subtractions are legitimate ordinary subtractions.

Using this observation, induction gives
\[
A_{2m+1}\le A_{2m+2}\le A_{2m+3}                            \tag{4}
\]
for every \(m\ge0\). The base case is \(A_1=1\le A_2=2\le A_3=7\). If (4) holds at \(m\), apply (3), with
\[
a=A_{2m+1},\quad b=A_{2m+2},\quad c=A_{2m+3},
\]
to (2). It follows that \(A_{2m+3}\le A_{2m+4}\). Equation (1), whose right side is a sum of nonnegative integers containing \(2A_{2m+4}\), then gives
\(A_{2m+4}\le A_{2m+5}\). This proves the induction step. Exactly the same argument, starting from \(B_1=3\le B_2=5\le B_3=19\), gives
\[
B_{2m+1}\le B_{2m+2}\le B_{2m+3}.                           \tag{5}
\]
Consequently, after embedding the integers in \(\mathbb R\), (2) is an equality with ordinary real subtraction for both sequences.

We now construct exact integral expressions for the errors \(B_n-eA_n\). For nonnegative integers \(a,b\), define
\[
J(a,b)=\int_0^1 e^x x^a(1-x)^b\,dx.                          \tag{6}
\]
Two elementary identities for these integrals will be used.

First, when \(r,s\ge1\), differentiation gives
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^x x^r(1-x)^s\right)
=e^x x^r(1-x)^s+r e^x x^{r-1}(1-x)^s-s e^x x^r(1-x)^{s-1}.
\]
The function inside the derivative vanishes at both endpoints, since \(r,s\ge1\). Integrating the derivative from \(0\) to \(1\) therefore yields
\[
J(r,s)+rJ(r-1,s)-sJ(r,s-1)=0.                                \tag{7}
\]

Second, for all \(a,b\ge0\), the pointwise identity
\[
x^{a+1}(1-x)^b=x^a(1-x)^b-x^a(1-x)^{b+1}
\]
gives
\[
J(a+1,b)=J(a,b)-J(a,b+1).                                    \tag{8}
\]

We use (7) and (8) to derive two more specialized identities. Applying (7) with \((r,s)=(m+1,m+2)\) gives
\[
J(m+1,m+2)+(m+1)J(m,m+2)-(m+2)J(m+1,m+1)=0.                 \tag{9}
\]
Applying it with \((r,s)=(m+2,m+2)\) gives
\[
J(m+2,m+2)+(m+2)J(m+1,m+2)-(m+2)J(m+2,m+1)=0.              \tag{10}
\]
By (8),
\[
J(m+2,m+1)=J(m+1,m+1)-J(m+1,m+2).                           \tag{11}
\]
Eliminating \(J(m+1,m+2)\) and \(J(m+2,m+1)\) from (9)--(11) yields
\[
\boxed{J(m+2,m+2)
=2(m+1)(m+2)J(m,m+2)-(2m+3)(m+2)J(m+1,m+1).}                \tag{12}
\]

For the second specialized identity, suppose \(m\ge1\). Equation (7), first at \((m,m+1)\) and then at \((m+1,m+1)\), gives
\[
J(m,m+1)+mJ(m-1,m+1)-(m+1)J(m,m)=0,                         \tag{13}
\]
\[
J(m+1,m+1)+(m+1)J(m,m+1)-(m+1)J(m+1,m)=0.                  \tag{14}
\]
Equation (8) gives
\[
J(m+1,m+1)=J(m,m+1)-J(m,m+2),                               \tag{15}
\]
\[
J(m+1,m)=J(m,m)-J(m,m+1).                                   \tag{16}
\]
Eliminating the two integrals appearing in (13)--(16) gives
\[
\boxed{-(m+1)J(m,m+2)
=(m+2)J(m+1,m+1)-m(m+1)J(m-1,m+1)+m(m+1)J(m,m).}            \tag{17}
\]
All these eliminations are ordinary linear algebra. For example, (13) expresses \(J(m,m+1)\) in terms of \(J(m-1,m+1)\) and \(J(m,m)\), while (15) and (16), substituted into (14), give the remaining relation containing \(J(m,m+2)\); rearrangement is exactly (17).

Define two error quantities, one for each parity:
\[
O_m=\frac{(-1)^{m+2}}{(m+1)!}J(m+1,m+1),                    \tag{18}
\]
\[
E_m=\frac{(-1)^{m+1}}{m!}J(m,m+2).                          \tag{19}
\]
Identity (12), together with \((m+2)!=(m+2)(m+1)!\) and
\((m+1)!=(m+1)m!\), gives
\[
O_{m+1}=2E_m+(2m+3)O_m.                                     \tag{20}
\]
Indeed, multiply (12) by \((-1)^{m+3}/(m+2)!\). The first term becomes
\[
2\frac{(-1)^{m+3}}{m!}J(m,m+2)=2E_m,
\]
since \((-1)^{m+3}=(-1)^{m+1}\), and the second becomes
\((2m+3)O_m\), since its extra minus sign changes \((-1)^{m+3}\) to \((-1)^{m+4}=(-1)^{m+2}\).

Likewise, multiplying (17) by the appropriate sign and factorial factors yields, for \(m\ge1\),
\[
E_m=(m+2)O_m-E_{m-1}-mO_{m-1}.                              \tag{21}
\]
This follows directly from (18), (19), the identity
\(m!=m(m-1)!\), and the fact that exponents of \(-1\) differing by two give the same sign.

We next identify the initial errors. Two elementary antiderivatives give the needed starting integrals. Since
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^x(-x^2+3x-3)\right)=e^x x(1-x),
\]
we have
\[
J(1,1)=\left[e^x(-x^2+3x-3)\right]_0^1=3-e.                 \tag{22}
\]
Also,
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^x(x^2-4x+5)\right)=e^x(1-x)^2,
\]
so
\[
J(0,2)=\left[e^x(x^2-4x+5)\right]_0^1=2e-5.                \tag{23}
\]
It follows from (18), (19), (22), and (23) that
\[
O_0=3-e=B_1-eA_1,
\]
and
\[
E_0=5-2e=B_2-eA_2.
\]

We claim that, for every \(m\ge0\),
\[
B_{2m+1}-eA_{2m+1}=O_m,                                     \tag{24}
\]
\[
B_{2m+2}-eA_{2m+2}=E_m.                                     \tag{25}
\]
The preceding calculation proves the claim at \(m=0\). Suppose (24) and (25) hold at \(m\). Subtracting \(e\) times the first equation in (1) from the second equation in (1) gives
\[
B_{2m+3}-eA_{2m+3}
=2(B_{2m+2}-eA_{2m+2})+(2m+3)(B_{2m+1}-eA_{2m+1}).
\]
By the induction hypothesis and (20), this is \(O_{m+1}\), proving (24) at \(m+1\).

Next use the real form of (2). Subtracting \(e\) times the recurrence for \(A\) from that for \(B\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
B_{2m+4}-eA_{2m+4}
={}&(m+3)(B_{2m+3}-eA_{2m+3})\\
&-(B_{2m+2}-eA_{2m+2})
-(m+1)(B_{2m+1}-eA_{2m+1}).
\end{aligned}
\]
The just-established odd case and the induction hypotheses turn the right side into
\[
(m+3)O_{m+1}-E_m-(m+1)O_m.
\]
Equation (21), with \(m+1\) in place of \(m\), says that this is exactly \(E_{m+1}\). Thus (25) also holds at \(m+1\), completing the induction.

We now prove that both kinds of error tend to zero. On \([0,1]\),
\[
0\le x^a\le1,\qquad 0\le(1-x)^b\le1,\qquad 0<e^x\le e.
\]
Therefore
\[
|J(a,b)|
\le \int_0^1\left|e^x x^a(1-x)^b\right|\,dx
\le \int_0^1 e\,dx=e.                                      \tag{26}
\]
Using \((m+1)!\ge m+1\), equations (18) and (26) imply
\[
|O_m|\le \frac{e}{(m+1)!}\le \frac{e}{m+1}.                 \tag{27}
\]
For \(m\ge1\), using \(m!\ge m\), equations (19) and (26) give
\[
|E_m|\le \frac{e}{m!}\le \frac{e}{m}.                      \tag{28}
\]
The right sides of (27) and (28) tend to zero, so
\[
O_m\longrightarrow0,
\qquad
E_m\longrightarrow0.                                       \tag{29}
\]

It follows from (24), (25), and (29) that the entire interleaved error sequence tends to zero:
\[
B_n-eA_n\longrightarrow0.                                   \tag{30}
\]
To see this explicitly, given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(M_o\) such that
\(|O_m|<\varepsilon\) for \(m\ge M_o\), and \(M_e\) such that
\(|E_m|<\varepsilon\) for \(m\ge M_e\). If \(n\) is sufficiently large and odd, write \(n=2m+1\); then \(m\ge M_o\), and (24) applies. If \(n\) is sufficiently large and even, write \(n=2m+2\); then \(m\ge M_e\), and (25) applies. Thus every sufficiently large \(n\), in either parity class, satisfies \(|B_n-eA_n|<\varepsilon\).

Finally, the denominators are positive. We already proved the monotonicity relations (4). Since \(A_1=1\) and \(A_2=2\), induction through the odd-even pairs gives
\[
A_{2m+1}>0,\qquad A_{2m+2}>0
\]
for every \(m\ge0\). Hence \(A_n\) is a positive integer for every \(n\ge1\), and in particular
\[
A_n\ge1.                                                     \tag{31}
\]
For such \(n\),
\[
\frac{B_n}{A_n}-e=\frac{B_n-eA_n}{A_n},
\]
and therefore, by (31),
\[
\left|\frac{B_n}{A_n}-e\right|
=\frac{|B_n-eA_n|}{A_n}
\le |B_n-eA_n|.                                              \tag{32}
\]
The right side tends to zero by (30). Consequently
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{A340737(n)}{A340738(n)}=e.}
\]
